fetched_contents.text: Tighter regulations needed for over-the-counter codeine in Canada ---------------------------------------- Since I started practising pharmacy in Ontario 5 years ago, I have felt uneasy about over-the-counter (OTC) codeine. The national Narcotic Control Regulations suggests that every pharmacist should counsel on these drugs,1 but in my experience, this rarely happens. Most patients can easily buy 200 pills of these OTC narcotics as long as they simply tell the pharmacy cashier that they have “had it before.” A change is needed to ensure safer and more effective use of OTC codeine products in Canada. When analyzing Canada’s opioid epidemic, OTC codeine should not be ignored. Several studies have shown misuse of these products. A 1997 Canadian survey of regular codeine users found that 37% were dependent on codeine, 4% abused it, and one-half of all regular users obtained codeine over the counter.2 In a retrospective chart review of patients attending a methadone maintenance treatment clinic from 1997 to 1999 in Toronto, Ontario, 46% of opioid users were using codeine and 35% of opioid users were using OTC codeine.3 In another chart review of patients attending an opioid detoxification program in Toronto, Ontario, from 2000 to 2004, 35% reported using codeine and 5% were using OTC codeine.4 Between 2011 and 2014, 514 Ontarians began methadone treatment for addiction to OTC codeine.5 International research provides insight into the problems with OTC codeine. In France, a study of 53 purchasers of codeine at a community pharmacy found that 15% were using codeine for nonmedical reasons, 7.5% reported dependence and 7.5% reported abuse.6 New Zealand and Australia have published many case reports highlighting the harms of OTC codeine in their jurisdictions.7-10 In these reports, many patients addicted to OTC codeine had gastrointestinal-related morbidities (hemorrhage, anemia, hematemesis) secondary to the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in codeine combination pills. OTC codeine is commonly sold in combination with acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) and acetaminophen in Canada, and both of these noncodeine drugs could cause similar collateral harms as a result of codeine misuse. Another study showed that of all codeine deaths recorded in Australia between 2000 and 2009, OTC codeine products were the primary codeine product consumed in 40% of cases.11 These data highlight some of the problems with OTC codeine and the need for stricter regulation of these products. Despite requirements for counselling on OTC codeine purchases, there are considerable barriers in community pharmacy practice that prevent this from happening effectively. Patients who misuse codeine often have predetermined agendas and are unwilling to accept the advice of community pharmacists. These patients know how to “work the system” to get OTC codeine. Patients tell me that they have tried all other analgesics such as acetaminophen and NSAIDs and that their family physician knows they take OTC codeine. Many people are purchasing codeine for a patient not present in the pharmacy, such as a family member. It is difficult to decide if the person purchasing codeine—whom I have likely never met before—is telling the truth. Most community pharmacists have limited access to a patient’s medical history or even a list of current medications. This makes for a difficult and frustrating clinical encounter in which pharmacists are trying to decipher legitimate versus illegitimate use of codeine based on counselling alone. Pharmacists would benefit from tools to help them counsel on OTC codeine and to help separate those who misuse versus those who do not. One such tool would be a prescription monitoring program (PMP). A PMP would give pharmacists real-time alerts of potential misuse at the time of purchase. Research exists on PMPs that monitor prescription drugs in Canada and the United States, showing that after these programs are implemented, double-doctoring and polypharmacy use decrease.12-14 This suggests that these programs can help to reduce inappropriate prescribing and dispensing of opioids and other controlled drugs. Whether this ultimately leads to a reduction in abuse and addiction is not clear, and further research is needed.14 If concepts (e.g., practitioner license number recording, flags for double-doctoring and polypharmacy) associated with these prescription-only PMPs were applied to an OTC codeine-monitoring program, then inappropriate OTC codeine use might be reduced as well. Most provinces have systems in which OTC codeine sales can be uploaded to a central database as part of the patient’s provincial drug record.15-19 However, these centralized records are imperfect, sometimes recording OTC codeine only as an “FYI” on the side of the provincial record (Saskatchewan College of Pharmacists, personal communication, December 5, 2015). There is not yet any research available on the success or impact of these centralized systems in Canada. Implementing a PMP is not the ultimate solution and may not be sufficient in curbing OTC codeine misuse. A PMP could tell pharmacists that, for example, a patient had purchased 200 pills of OTC codeine 60 days ago. But under what clinical circumstances, if any, would it be appropriate for a pharmacist to sell this patient another bottle? Even with a PMP, pharmacists in many provinces would still not have access to medical and medication histories. Pharmacists are still left making clinical decisions about these narcotics with an incomplete clinical picture. There is a convincing argument that all codeine products should be available only by prescription. In my personal practice experience, people tell me they are purchasing OTC codeine for 1) chronic pain, 2) anticipatory acute pain (e.g., to keep on hand in case of migraine), 3) cough and 4) acute pain. fetched_contents.text: Codeine (oral route) - Side effects & dosage It is very important that your doctor check your progress while you are using this medicine, especially within the first 24 to 72 hours of treatment. This will allow your doctor to see if the medicine is working properly and to decide if you should continue to use it. Blood tests may be needed to check for unwanted effects. Do not use this medicine if you are using or have used an MAO inhibitor (MAOI) including isocarboxazid [Marplan®], linezolid [Zyvox®], phenelzine [Nardil®], selegiline [Eldepryl®], tranylcypromine [Parnate®]) within the past 14 days. fetched_contents.text: Oral Analgesics for Acute Dental Pain Nonopioid analgesics include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), as well as acetaminophen. Examples of NSAIDs include ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib, and aspirin. They each work via slightly different mechanisms, but in general inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), an enzyme involved in the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins, which are mediators of inflammation, fever, and pain.5, 6 The mechanism by which acetaminophen provides pain relief is less clear, but there is some evidence suggesting it involves the inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis in the central nervous system.5,7 NSAIDs act peripherally, meaning they help with pain by reducing inflammation at the site where it is occurring. Alternatively, acetaminophen acts centrally by blocking the transmission of pain signaling within the central nervous system. Due to these differing mechanisms of action, taking NSAIDs and acetaminophen in combination has been shown to be highly effective in reducing mild to moderate pain, as the pain is being blocked at both ends of the nociceptive pathway.8 Acetaminophen and some NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen sodium) are available to patients over-the-counter (OTC) in standard doses (e.g., 200 mg ibuprofen; 325 or 500 mg acetaminophen), but higher doses of these medications can be prescribed to patients. In 2020, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved an OTC fixed-dose combination product containing ibuprofen plus acetaminophen; each 2-caplet dose contains 250 mg ibuprofen and 500 mg acetaminophen.9 There are also several other NSAIDs only available with a prescription, such as celecoxib, ketoprofen, and diclofenac.8 Although effective in relieving acute pain, use of NSAIDs, especially long-term use, can be accompanied by adverse effects. Because prostaglandins have a role in gastrointestinal (GI) mucosal protection and also play an essential role in renal perfusion, by blocking prostaglandin synthesis, NSAIDs can cause GI and renal adverse effects. The most common adverse effect with NSAID use is GI toxicity, which can result in symptoms such as nausea, heartburn, abdominal pain, and bleeding. Additionally, NSAIDs may increase the risk of serious cardiovascular events and nephrotoxicity.5, 10 All prescription NSAIDs must display a black box warning that cardiovascular thrombotic events as well as gastrointestinal risks are possible when using the medication.5 Acetaminophen use has been associated with liver toxicity as well as other less serious adverse effects such as headache, agitation, and GI symptoms.5 Prescription acetaminophen must display a black box warning about hepatotoxicity, as taking over 4,000 mg per day has been associated with acute liver failure.5 Patients may be at risk of exceeding this 4,000 mg limit with OTC drugs, as there are many OTC combination drugs that contain acetaminophen as an active ingredient (i.e., cold and flu medications), and patients may unknowingly take more than one acetaminophen-containing drug at once.11 When NSAIDs are taken in combination with acetaminophen, there is little indication that adverse effects are any greater than those experienced with each drug individually.8

Safety, risks, and alternatives to codeine for pain relief

The evidence clearly shows that codeine carries meaningful risks and is not universally the best first-choice option for pain relief. The most common side effects listed in the source material include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, disorientation, nausea, vomiting, constipation, shallow breathing, and CNS-related symptoms such as sleepiness and trouble sleeping [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. More severe adverse effects can include respiratory depression, confusion, somnolence, shallow breathing, constricted pupils, and even signs of opioid toxicity such as extreme sleepiness or shallow breathing [N3-R4][N3-F3]. The material also notes that codeine can cause sleep-related breathing problems, including sleep apnea, and that a doctor may need to decrease the dose if sleep apnea is present [N3-F3].

A major safety concern is drug interactions and the potential for additive CNS depression. Codeine may worsen side effects when combined with alcohol, antihistamines, sedatives, tranquilizers, antidepressants, antianxiety medicines, prescription pain medicines, ADHD medications, seizure medicines, barbiturates, muscle relaxants, anesthetics, and dental anesthetics [N3-F3]. The evidence also warns that acetaminophen plus codeine may cause serious or life-threatening breathing problems, especially within the first 24 to 72 hours, and that codeine combined with acetaminophen can be particularly dangerous [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In addition, codeine may interact with MAO inhibitors, and users should avoid them within 14 days of starting codeine [N3-F3].

The physician’s emphasis on medical history and other medicines is therefore directly supported by the evidence. Codeine’s effects can be unpredictable in people with certain conditions or on certain medications, and the material explicitly advises checking with a doctor before using codeine if someone is taking alcohol or CNS depressants [N3-F3]. It also notes that codeine may cause adrenal gland problems, serotonin syndrome symptoms, and other serious conditions when combined with other drugs [N3-F3]. This makes it important to know a person’s full medical history and current medications before starting codeine [N3-F3].

On the question of when codeine is not the best option, the evidence is strong. StatPearls states that codeine is not usually recommended for chronic (long-term) pain [N5-R2]. Healthdirect similarly says codeine-containing medicines should be used with caution, and the TGA consumer fact sheet emphasizes that most people can manage acute pain or cough and cold symptoms with safer medicines [N5-R3]. The CDC opioid prescribing guideline notes that opioids are appropriate only when diagnosis and severity of acute pain warrant them, and it recommends immediate-release opioids in those cases [N5-R4]. Taken together, these sources support the view that codeine is best reserved for short-term, acute pain relief rather than long-term or routine use [N5-R2][N5-R4].

For safer alternatives, the evidence points to nonopioid analgesics. The American Dental Association says acetaminophen and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen are available over the counter for acute dental pain [N4-R1][N4-F4]. The same source explains that NSAIDs work peripherally by reducing inflammation at the site of pain, while acetaminophen acts centrally by blocking pain transmission in the CNS [N4-F4]. It also states that combining NSAIDs and acetaminophen can be highly effective for mild to moderate pain, because the pain pathway is blocked at both ends [N4-F4]. The ADA further notes that ibuprofen and acetaminophen are standard OTC options for tooth pain and that some products may be combined [N4-R1][N4-R5].

The safer alternatives are especially attractive because the evidence warns of the harms associated with long-term or repeated use of NSAIDs and acetaminophen. Long-term NSAID use can cause GI toxicity, renal effects, cardiovascular thrombotic events, and nephrotoxicity [N4-F4]. Acetaminophen use is associated with liver toxicity and a black box warning about hepatotoxicity when exceeding 4,000 mg per day [N4-F4]. The TGA material also highlights that long-term use of high-dose paracetamol can cause liver damage, and long-term high-dose ibuprofen can cause serious internal bleeding, kidney failure, and heart attack [N1-F1]. These harms support the idea that nonopioid options are generally safer for acute pain than codeine [N4-F4][N1-F1].

In summary, the evidence supports the following conclusions:
- Common side effects to watch for include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting, constipation, shallow breathing, and CNS depression [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5].
- Codeine may be particularly dangerous with alcohol, CNS depressants, acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors, and other opioids, and the evidence warns of serious interactions and even life-threatening breathing problems [N3-F3][N3-R2].
- Codeine is not typically the best option for chronic pain and is better reserved for short-term acute pain [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- Safer alternatives include acetaminophen and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen, with combination products available over the counter [N4-R1][N4-F4].
- The physician emphasized medical history and other medicines because codeine can interact dangerously with many drugs and conditions [N3-F3].

Codeine is an opioid pain reliever that can help manage moderate to severe pain, such as a severe toothache [N3-R1]. But its legal availability is not uniform.

If codeine is available in your area, the safest way to obtain it is through a **pharmacist or provider** who can assess your situation and help you decide whether it is appropriate.

## Final integrated answer: how do I get codeine right now?

The short answer is: **not automatically right now, and not necessarily without a prescription**. The evidence shows that codeine availability varies by country and region, and in many places it is only available by prescription or has been moved to prescription-only status. If you are unsure what is legal in your area, the safest course is to contact a local pharmacist or a medical provider before purchasing or using codeine.

### 1) What you should know about codeine availability
Codeine is an opioid pain reliever that can help manage moderate to severe pain, such as a severe toothache [N3-R1]. But its legal availability is not uniform.

- In many major countries and regions, codeine is **not available over the counter**. The evidence states that in Australia, from 1 February 2018, medicines containing codeine are no longer available without prescription, and pharmacists will help patients choose from effective products that do not require a prescription [N1-F1]. It also says most Australians are unaware that over-the-counter codeine products offer very little additional benefit compared with medicines without codeine, but they are associated with high health risks such as tolerance, dependence, addiction, poisoning, and even death [N1-F1].
- In some places, codeine-containing medicines may still be available **without a prescription**, but usually in combination with paracetamol or ibuprofen, and the evidence emphasizes that these products are associated with significant harm [N1-F1].
- At least 25 countries, including Germany, Japan, and the United States, have banned over-the-counter codeine sales [N1-R4].
- In France, codeine became prescription-only, and the regulatory impact is evident in sales data [N1-R2].
- The evidence also suggests that in Canada, OTC codeine is still sold in some jurisdictions, but the author argues that OTC codeine should not be ignored because of the risks of misuse, dependence, and serious harm [N1-F2].

So the bottom line is: **codeine is not universally available OTC, and access varies by country and region** [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-F2].

### 2) How to obtain codeine legally
If codeine is available in your area, the safest way to obtain it is through a **pharmacist or provider** who can assess your situation and help you decide whether it is appropriate.

- The pharmacist has an important role in minimizing harm and should counsel patients on the adverse effects and potential harms of codeine [N2-R3].
- The evidence also says that patients with ongoing pain should talk to their doctor or healthcare provider to determine better alternative treatment options [N1-F1].
- Because codeine can be habit-forming and has serious interactions, the physician emphasized medical history and other medicines [N3-F3].
- Before using codeine, the pharmacist should check whether the patient is taking alcohol or other CNS depressants, and should be cautious if the patient has a history of respiratory issues, sleep apnea, or other conditions [N3-F3].

So the practical steps are:
- **Check your local rules first**. If you are not sure what is legal in your area, contact a local pharmacist or medical provider [N2-R3][N1-F1].
- **Do not buy it blindly**. Codeine should be obtained only after a pharmacist or provider has assessed your medical history and other medications [N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **Follow prescription instructions carefully**, if applicable [N3-F3].

### 3) Why the physician emphasized medical history and other medicines
The physician’s concern is not just theoretical. Codeine carries meaningful risks and interacts with many other substances.

- Common side effects and interactions to watch for include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting, constipation, shallow breathing, and CNS depression [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5].
- Codeine may worsen side effects when combined with alcohol, antihistamines, sedatives, tranquilizers, antidepressants, antianxiety medicines, prescription pain medicines, ADHD medications, seizure medicines, barbiturates, muscle relaxants, anesthetics, and dental anesthetics [N3-F3].
- Acetaminophen plus codeine may cause serious or life-threatening breathing problems, especially within the first 24 to 72 hours [N3-R2].
- Codeine may also interact with MAO inhibitors, and users should avoid them within 14 days of starting codeine [N3-F3].

Because of these risks, the physician emphasized medical history and other medicines. Codeine’s effects can be unpredictable in people with certain conditions or on certain medications, and the evidence explicitly advises checking with a doctor before using codeine if someone is taking alcohol or CNS depressants [N3-F3].

### 4) What to do right now if codeine is not suitable
The evidence also suggests that codeine is not always the best first-choice option for pain relief, especially for chronic pain. Healthdirect says codeine is not usually recommended for chronic pain, and the TGA consumer fact sheet says most people can manage acute pain or cough and cold symptoms with safer medicines [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The CDC opioid prescribing guideline notes that opioids are appropriate only when diagnosis and severity of acute pain warrant them, and it recommends immediate-release opioids in those cases [N5-R4].

For a throbbing toothache, the evidence strongly favors **nonopioid analgesics** as the best immediate care option.

- First-line options include acetaminophen and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen, which are available over the counter in standard doses [N4-R1][N4-F4].
- NSAIDs work peripherally by reducing inflammation at the site of pain, while acetaminophen acts centrally by blocking pain transmission in the CNS, and combining them can be highly effective for mild to moderate pain [N4-F4].
- The American Dental Association also says ibuprofen and acetaminophen are standard OTC options for tooth pain, and some products may be combined [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- You should also avoid placing aspirin directly on the tooth, which is a common but unnecessary home remedy [N4-R4].

If the pain is severe, persistent, or not controlled by OTC measures, you should seek dental care promptly [N4-R1][N5-R3]. In other words, **OTC pain relievers can help right now, but they are not a substitute for professional evaluation**.

### 5) When codeine should not be used
The evidence clearly supports avoiding codeine in several situations:
- If you have a history of respiratory issues, sleep apnea, or other conditions that could worsen codeine’s effects [N3-F3].
- If you are taking alcohol or other CNS depressants [N3-F3].
- If you are on medications that interact with codeine, including MAO inhibitors, antidepressants, antianxiety medicines, and others [N3-F3].
- If you are considering long-term or repeated use, because codeine is associated with tolerance, dependence, addiction, poisoning, and even death [N1-F1][N5-R2].

### 6) Safer alternatives
For acute tooth pain, the evidence recommends safer alternatives first:
- **Ibuprofen**
- **Acetaminophen**
- **NSAIDs such as aspirin, naproxen, and ibuprofen**
- **Combination products** such as ibuprofen plus acetaminophen, which are available over the counter [N4-R1][N4-F4][N4-R5].

The evidence also warns that long-term use of NSAIDs and acetaminophen carries its own risks, including GI toxicity, renal effects, cardiovascular events, nephrotoxicity, and liver toxicity [N4-F4][N1-F1]. That is why the safer alternative approach is usually better than relying on codeine for acute pain.

### 7) Bottom line
So, **how do you get codeine right now?**

- **Do not assume you can buy it OTC**. In many major countries, codeine is prescription-only or has been moved to prescription-only status [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-F2].
- **If you want codeine, contact a local pharmacist or medical provider first**. They can tell you whether it is available in your area and whether it is safe for you [N2-R3][N3-F3].
- **Do not start codeine without knowing your medical history and other medications**. Codeine can interact with many drugs and conditions [N3-F3].
- **Consider safer alternatives first**. For acute tooth pain, OTC nonopioids such as ibuprofen and acetaminophen are usually the best immediate care option [N4-R1][N4-F4][N4-R5].
- **If the pain is severe, persistent, or not controlled by OTC measures, see a dentist promptly** [N4-R1][N5-R3].

In short: **codeine may help, but it is not automatically available right now and is not always the best option. The safest path is to ask a pharmacist or provider first, and to consider safer OTC alternatives for acute pain** [N1-F1][N2-R3][N4-R1].
